newsitem.title: MOROCCO: King Hassan opens Moroccan parliament session.
newsitem.headline: King Hassan opens Moroccan parliament session.

text.p: King Hassan opened the Moroccan parliament's autumn session on Friday with a pledge to put his personal backing behind free and fair polling in elections expected to be held in the first half of next year.

"Be sure that I will put my personal weight and my constitutional power (to ensure) that the next elections in this country will take place in the best conditions of transparency and credibility," he told MPs in the 333-seat parliament.
He said: "I have had enough of hearing that elections in my country were not credible or clean."
Morocco is shortly to change its parliamentary system following a referendum on September 13 which overwhelmingly backed King Hassan's proposals for constitutional reform.

Under the proposed change, the existing sole house will become the lower assembly, directly elected, while a new upper house will be created. Its members will be appointed through indirect elections, mainly through professional, council and union bodies.
The new upper house will have power to force a vote of no-confidence in the government and topple it.
King Hassan told MPs he would confer soon with leaders of political parties including the opposition, which holds 125 seats in the present parliament.
In his 14-minute speech, the king stressed the need for greater representation from regions and urged existing MPs to adopt by consensus the legislation already before the house.

Speaking about changes in political power between parties, the king said: "Is it in the interests of our democracy to have alternation with four or five voices, or to have a real alternation between two blocs balanced in the centre by another."
He said he would discuss these ideas in detail with party leaders, adding that changes in political power should bring new ideas and methods to parliament.

In an apparent reference to neighbouring Algeria, King Hassan said he preferred there should be several parties rather than a proliferation of "small parasitical groups which invade the political scene...like in countries which have the same population as ours and have more than 40 parties."
The king gave no date for the elections which will also take place in the disputed Western Sahara.
